Pipeline Team For Vets For Partners News Contact Get updates They're family. Their medicine should be familiar. Familiar translates proven human medicines into novel therapeutics for the animals who share our lives, designed to reach every pet, through every veterinary clinic. See our pipeline Contact us The opportunity Our pets get the same diseases we do. They deserve the same breakthroughs. Dogs and cats develop many of the same cancers, immune disorders, and other serious diseases that affect people, but the medicines available to treat them haven’t kept pace. For families and veterinarians, that means facing devastating diagnoses with too few options. We believe pets deserve medicines that can change the course of disease. Familiar exists to help make that possible. Our approach Built on human science. Developed for pets. Familiar takes proven human drug candidates with validated targets and established safety data, and translates them into novel therapeutics for companion animals. We partner with the pharma and biotech companies that developed these medicines. From there, we take on the veterinary development work: animal-specific research, clinical studies and the path to FDA approval. And because the biology is shared, the science flows both ways. Dogs and cats develop these diseases naturally, making companion animal clinical programs a powerful source of early efficacy signal for human drug development. We are launching a clinical study to evaluate FAM-010 in dogs recently diagnosed with hemangiosarcoma. FAM-010 is a new form of doxorubicin, designed to deliver more medicine to tumors while reducing exposure to healthy tissue, so dogs can receive more of the treatment they need. See if your dog qualifies Refer a patient → FAM-010 is an investigational drug and is not approved by FDA. For partners → OUR ORIGIN A search for one better treatment became a platform. Lily Iorns 7.2.13 – 10.6.2021 In 2020, our co-founder Elizabeth received the kind of news every pet owner dreads. Her French Bulldog, Lily, had been diagnosed with a terminal brain tumor. As a cancer biologist who had spent her career at the frontier of human oncology, Elizabeth knew what modern targeted therapy could do. But for canine glioma, no such option existed. The standard of care hadn't changed in years. The experience exposed something larger than one diagnosis. Companion-animal therapeutics has historically attracted a fraction of the R&D investment that human medicine commands.
